extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, judges, and law students studying patent infringement doctrine
extracted.subtask_description: Legal guidance on how to determine infringement of patents (process, product, and principle-based patents), including evidentiary rules, tests of substantial identity, and when defendant variations amount to piracy or constitute a new patentable invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process vs. manufacture (product) distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the patent covers a process of manufacture, infringement inquiry is whether the defendant used the patentee's process; where the invention is an entirely new manufacture, it is immaterial by what process it is produced — making the same thing is infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘‘In such cases, where the object to be accomplished is open to the public, notwithstanding the patent, provided it can be accomplished in several modes, which, as processes, are substantially different, an infringement must be in respect of the process used by the patentee. ... Or, to state this in other words, where the invention, or subject-matter of the patent, is an entirely new manufacture, it is immaterial by what process it is produced, since the infringement must consist in making the same thing, whether by one process or another.’’ (examples and discussion throughout §§313–314)

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof on the plaintiff to show process infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: The plaintiff always bears the burden of proving that his process has been infringed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘‘The burden of proof is always on the plaintiff, to show that his process has been infringed; and in the absence of direct evidence, the similarity of the effect produced will generally be sufficient to establish an infringement, and if this is aided by evidence of the use of similar apparatus, the presumption of a use of the same process will be still stronger.’’ (§314; supported by Hall v. Boot example)

rubrics_metrics.name: Similarity of structure/appearance is presumptive evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Similarity in appearance and structure is presumptive evidence that two articles were made in the same way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘‘The rule was laid down by Lord Ellenborough, that the similarity of structure of two things is presumptive evidence of their being made in the same way.’’ (illustrated by Huddart v. Grimshaw and cases where witnesses opined that similar effect and structure meant same process)

rubrics_metrics.name: Strength of inference from identical article varies with possible alternative processes
rubrics_metrics.description: The probative force of identity of the manufactured article depends on whether it appears possible or probable that the article could have been made by a different, independent process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘‘The identity of the manufactured article is, with all the other circumstances, competent evidence, from which the jury are to infer that it was made by the process of the patentee; although there may be cases, where, from the nature of the article, this proof would be less strong, according as it appeared to be possible or probable that the article could be made by more than one process.’’ (§314)

rubrics_metrics.name: When specification limits claim to a particular mode, mere production may not prove infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: If the specification describes a particular mode of carrying out the invention, mere production of an article with similar results does not necessarily prove use of that specified mode.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: where the specification stated the invention to relate to 'a mode of manufacturing candles by the application of two or more plaited wicks in each candle' and set out the mode at length, the mere production of a candle in which the wicks turned outward in burning was held to be no evidence of infringement. (per totam curiam cited in §314)

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventions that are applications of a principle: focus on substantial identity of principle and its application
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the subject-matter is the application of a principle (a law of nature or rule of practice), the infringement inquiry asks whether the defendant has substantially applied the same principle and applied it in the same way; means, machinery, or modifications matter only insofar as they affect the identity of the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘‘A clear idea is to be formed of the object of the patent ... the question, on an infringement, will be as to the substantial identity of the principle, and of the application of the principle; and consequently the means, machinery, forms, or modifications of matter made use of will be material, only so far as they affect the identity of the application.’’ (§316–317; examples: Forsyth, self-adjusting leverage in chairs, welding by pressure, Clegg measuring gas)

rubrics_metrics.name: Mode of carrying a principle into effect grants protection against other modes applying same principle
rubrics_metrics.description: If the patentee has invented some mode of carrying a principle into effect, he can protect himself against other modes that apply the same principle — variations in apparatus or form that still apply the same principle are piracy of the original invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘‘You cannot take out a patent for a principle; you may ... for a principle coupled with the mode of carrying the principle into effect ... if you have invented some mode ... then you are entitled to protect yourself from all other modes of carrying the same principle into effect, that being treated by the jury as piracy of your original invention.’’ (Neilson and related discussion in §§319–320; Neilson v. Harford example)

rubrics_metrics.name: Superior or improved apparatus does not avoid infringement if it applies the same principle
rubrics_metrics.description: A defendant's apparatus may be a great improvement over what the patentee described, yet still infringe if it applies the same principle as claimed and falls within the specification's scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Neilson: defendant's apparatus was superior but held an infringement because it applied heated air in the close vessel between blowing apparatus and furnace — ‘‘it is the application of heated air ... and therefore ... it would be an infringement of it.’’ (§319)

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination claims: claiming a combination can be valid and use of the same combination may infringe even if components were previously separate
rubrics_metrics.description: A combination of known elements can be the subject of a patent; using that same combination (even if parts were previously separately used) may be infringement, and minor differences in arrangement need not avoid liability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: patent claiming combination of a blast and an exhaust in ventilating millstones held valid and infringed even though blast and exhaust had been used separately before; use in a mill with different stone rotation was still infringement. (§319)

rubrics_metrics.name: Variations that show a different application (different law/rule of science) constitute no infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: If the defendant's variations show that the application of the principle is materially varied — i.e., some other law or rule of science or practice is employed in place of that which the patentee claims as the essence — there is no infringement and the defendant may have made a substantial invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘‘But of course where the variations adopted by the defendant show that the application of the principle is varied, that some other law or rule of science, or of practice, is made to take the place of that which the patentee claims as the essence of his invention, then there will be no infringement, but a substantial invention.’’ (§320; Barber v. Grace cited)

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantive invention by defendant is a test for non-infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: If the defendant, without borrowing from the patentee, has invented a new mode of accomplishing the same object — i.e., a patentable substantive invention — then he is entitled to his patent and does not infringe the earlier patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘‘There may be many different modes of obtaining the same object; and consequently if, after a patent has been obtained for a particular thing, another party, without borrowing from that patent, has invented a new mode of accomplishing the same object, he will be entitled to a patent for his discovery.’’ (§322; Walton v. Potter quoted)

rubrics_metrics.name: Identity of the 'essence' or 'substantial identity' is the key test
rubrics_metrics.description: In principle-based patents the court looks to the substantial identity respecting that which constitutes the essence of the invention — the application of the principle — and treats only substantial identity as infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘‘The substantial identity, therefore, that is to be looked to, in cases of this kind, respects that which constitutes the essence of the invention, viz., the application of the principle. If the mode ... adopted by the defendant still shows only that the principle admits of the same application in a variety of forms ... the jury will be authorized to treat such mode as a piracy ...’’ (§320)

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert testimony and practical judgment may be unnecessary but can support conclusion on substantial identity
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts may conclude infringement from the record and practical comparison without resorting to expert testimony, though expert evidence can support the finding that two processes embody the same essential idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mowry v. Whitney: ‘‘It hardly seems necessary to resort to the opinions of experts in order to reach the conclusion that the process of the defendant is only formally different from that of Whitney, while the essential element of the two processes is the same. But ... the testimony of the experts ... clearly supports such a conclusion.’’ (§319a)
